passage: In Kasauli's narrow market, Mehak's aunt ran a small pickle stall, and Mehak, twenty and home for the holidays, had big plans for it. She'd been watching interviews with famous founders. They all woke at four, skipped breakfast, and said "never keep a fallback". So Mehak set her alarm for four, stopped eating before noon, and told her aunt to stop supplying the dhaba so they could go all in on online orders. Her cousin Anand, who ran the dhaba's kitchen, listened over chai. "Didn't the man with the pickle website in Solan do exactly that?" he asked. "He shut down last year." Mehak waved it off. The founders on her screen had done it and succeeded. The ones who'd done it and failed didn't give interviews.

qa.q: What did Mehak tell her aunt to stop doing?
qa.a: Mehak told her aunt to stop supplying the dhaba so they could go all in on online orders.

qa.q: Why does Mehak trust the founders' habits so completely?
qa.a: Every founder on her screen had those habits and succeeded, so the habits look like the cause, while those who failed stay unseen.

qa.q: What could Mehak do before changing the stall's business?
qa.a: She could look into sellers like the Solan man who tried the same thing and failed, and test online orders while keeping the dhaba supply.

qa.q: How might Mehak's aunt be affected if she stops supplying the dhaba?
qa.a: Her aunt could lose steady income from the dhaba because of habits copied from interviews.

grounding: A student copies famous founders' habits and plans, brushing aside a nearby example of someone with the same habits who failed.

passage: Felix had printed a list and taped it above his desk in the Munich flat: "Habits of Great Founders". Sleep five hours. Drop out when your idea takes off. Never listen to doubters. He'd got all of it from a bestselling book about famous startups. His flatmate Aiko, who studied statistics, read it while waiting for the kettle. "Who wrote down the habits of the founders who failed?" she asked. "Nobody writes books about them," said Felix. "Exactly," she said. "How many people sleep five hours and ignore doubters and still go broke?" Felix frowned. He thought of his cousin's food-delivery idea, which had eaten two years and all his savings. Same habits. No book. He didn't take the list down. But that night he slept eight hours.

qa.q: What was the title of the list above Felix's desk?
qa.a: Habits of Great Founders.

qa.q: Why did the list seem convincing to Felix?
qa.a: Felix felt inspired by a book about famous startups, where every example had the habits and the success together, making the habits look like the cause.

qa.q: What question from Aiko could Felix keep using?
qa.a: He could keep asking how many people did the same thing and still failed, before copying any habit from a success story.

qa.q: How does Aiko's statistics training shape the way she sees the list?
qa.a: Aiko looks for the missing group, the founders who failed, so she sees the list as one-sided rather than a recipe.

grounding: A student copies habits from successful founders until a flatmate asks about everyone with the same habits who failed.

passage: At the college incubation cell, Amandeep presented his plan for a campus laundry pickup service to the mentor panel. "We're following the founder playbook," he said. "Launch before it's ready, spend big on ads, skip the market research, like the famous ones did." Jatin, the final-year mentor on the panel, leaned forward. "How many campus startups has the cell funded in the last five years?" Amandeep didn't know. Jatin pulled up the list: forty-two. Three were still running. "Most of the other thirty-nine followed the same playbook," Jatin said. "You only know the three because they give talks at orientation." Amandeep stared at the screen. He had sat in those talks, taking notes. The other thirty-nine had never been invited.

qa.q: How many campus startups has the cell funded in the last five years?
qa.a: Forty-two, and three were still running.

qa.q: Why did the playbook feel like the right plan to Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep felt confident because he had only heard the three successful founders at orientation talks, so their habits seemed like the reason they won.

qa.q: What should Amandeep look at before launching?
qa.a: He should study why the other thirty-nine closed, and maybe do the market research the playbook told him to skip.

qa.q: How might the founders of the thirty-nine closed startups see the orientation talks?
qa.a: They might feel the talks give a lopsided picture, since they followed similar steps and were never invited to speak.

grounding: A student copies a famous founder playbook until a mentor shows most funded startups with the same habits failed.

passage:
Dear Eshaan,
You asked how the new routine is going. Well, I've read every interview with the three founders I admire, and I'm copying their habits. Up at five like the first one. Same black T-shirt every day like the second, to save "decision energy." No lectures after lunch, because the third one said college slows you down. Cold showers, a gratitude journal, no weekend outings.
I'm three weeks in. My marks in the mid-sem dipped, but that's temporary. They all struggled before they made it.
Mamu asked me, his only nephew, an odd question on the phone yesterday: how many people wake at five, wear the same T-shirt and skip lectures, and never become founders? I said that's not the point. But I haven't stopped thinking about it.
Anyway, how's your placement prep?
Chinmay

qa.q: What time does Chinmay now wake up?
qa.a: He wakes up at five, like the first founder.

qa.q: Why does copying these habits feel like a sensible plan to Chinmay?
qa.a: He admires the three founders and believes their habits caused their success, so repeating them feels like the surest way to follow them, even as his marks dip.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do with Mamu's question before continuing the routine?
qa.a: He could honestly think about the many people with the same habits who never became founders, and keep only the habits that actually help him, like protecting his lectures.

qa.q: How might Eshaan react reading about the skipped lectures?
qa.a: Eshaan might be worried about the dipped marks and wonder whether the black T-shirt and cold showers are really what made those founders succeed.

grounding: A student's letter shows him copying famous founders' habits without noticing that many with the same habits failed.

passage:
Wasim, you asked why I stopped the "billionaire morning." Okay. I'm Suraj, I'm twenty, and for two months I lived like the top five founders in a list someone shared.
Journal at dawn. Meditate. No breakfast. Read one book a week. Skip anything that "wasn't building the empire," which for me meant skipping my part-time job at the phone shop.
One evening my friend's sister, who works at a startup incubator in Pune, came over. I proudly showed her my routine. She laughed kindly and said, "Young man, half the founders I see do all of this. Most of them shut down within two years. You just don't read interviews with those ones."
That hit me. I'd only ever seen the winners. The ones with the same habits who failed were invisible to me.
I kept the book a week. I went back to the phone shop.

qa.q: Which job did Suraj skip during the two months?
qa.a: He skipped his part-time job at the phone shop.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel when the incubator worker described the founders she sees?
qa.a: He felt hit, suddenly realising he had only seen the winners, and that failed founders with the same habits had been invisible to him.

qa.q: Which choices did Suraj make after that evening, and why do they make sense?
qa.a: He kept the book a week, which he found useful, and went back to the phone shop, since the other habits didn't guarantee success.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Suraj's two months after hearing this?
qa.a: Wasim might find it funny and a little relieving, understanding that a list of winners' habits leaves out everyone who did the same and failed.

grounding: A student recalls copying famous founders' habits until he realised many with the same habits failed and were simply never seen.
